segments.t: Hi, I'm Alice, and welcome to T L D R Daily, your quick tour of today's tech news.
And I'm Michael. Today is heavy on data exposure and supply chain risk, with a few Dev Ops and A I platform stories that matter for how teams build and ship.

Let's start with the biggest breach. A filing with the U S health department now puts the iRhythm breach at about eight point two million people. The T L D R Information Security newsletter says hackers got into third-party-hosted business applications back in June, demanded a ransom, and threatened to leak the stolen data.

The exposed data is broad. Names, contact details, dates of birth, account and device identifiers, insurance numbers, and service dates. iRhythm says it has no evidence of identity theft and found no impact on medical devices.
Absolutely.

Insurance numbers and birth dates are hard to change, so affected people should expect convincing phishing that quotes real details. And third parties keep showing up. The same newsletter says Japan Airlines is notifying about ninety-two thousand customers after a vendor running its reservation and check-in systems was breached.

For most of them it was names and flight details, but for about two thousand customers it also included passport numbers. Separately, a leak site released data on more than forty thousand Homeland Security employees, taken from an Okta instance, though Okta says it was not breached.

Next, credentials. A researcher scanned about seven point two five million public Gitee repositories and found twenty-six thousand four hundred working cloud and A I credentials, according to the Information Security newsletter.
That includes more than nine thousand Alibaba Cloud access key pairs, more than three thousand Deep Seek keys, and about thirteen hundred Open A I keys. These are live keys, not old test strings.
Totally, rotate those keys today.

Related, the same newsletter says a scanner has impersonated thirty-two A I bots, from Open A I, Anthropic, Perplexity and others, since late September. It probes about ninety paths for passwords and keys. On one October day, forty-eight percent of protected organizations received that traffic.
Most requests failed or were blocked. Now a heist. The general T L D R newsletter says Binance suspended transactions after a hack the exchange put at around six point three billion dollars.
It reports the attack appears to be the work of a North Korean group. Tether and Circle froze some of the stolen assets, and Binance's founder says user funds are safe.
Wow, that's a lot.

Now the Linux kernel. Anthropic researchers found a use-after-free flaw in the T C P handshake, scored nine point eight out of ten. A race condition can cause memory corruption, kernel memory reads, or crashes. Red Hat rates it lower, because the race is complex to exploit.
Right, so patch when your vendor ships the fix, but don't panic.
Now supply chain. The Dev Ops newsletter points to a Wiz write-up on pull request target attacks against Git Hub Actions. Git Hub's changes this year make them harder, but gaps remain.
So where are the holes that still work for attackers today?

Outdated checkout versions, script injection, and unprotected triggers like issue comments. Pinning actions to old commit hashes from before the July backport release bypasses the new protections entirely. The default policy also doesn't cover private repositories.
Exactly, that's the part to watch.

There's a defensive move too. Git Hub launched a package firewall in public preview for Enterprise Cloud. The Information Security newsletter says it sits between coding agents, C I hosts and registries, with cooldown periods, advisory checks, and blocks on attestation downgrades.

Dev Ops also flagged Git Hub Agentic Workflows going generally available, using coding agents inside Actions for issue triage and C I failure analysis. And the I T newsletter says Git Hub is adding four million cores, after seven point four billion commits in September, five times last year.
Definitely, agents are driving that volume.

One more research story. Hacktron showed how it could have backdoored Bash. A forge for G N U software passed an email address unescaped into a shell command, which gave code execution on the backend.

They used that foothold to impersonate the Bash maintainer and reach an S S H key page that could have allowed pushes upstream. The Free Software Foundation fixed all twenty-six reported flaws. The lesson is to treat email addresses as untrusted input.
Good point, input is input.

On the platform side, Kubernetes launched a Workload Conformance Working Group to write a shared specification and tests for how workloads behave at runtime. It aims for a stable first specification within two to three release cycles.

And a Git Ops story. One Argo C D hub managed thirty-four clusters across twenty-two Amazon accounts, and onboarding reportedly fell from four days to one point seven hours. D B O S also reports scaling durable workflows to one million per second on Postgres across fifty shards.

Moving to the I T newsletter. Oracle plans usage-based A I charges alongside Fusion subscriptions, so customers pay as automated tasks complete rather than per seat. It describes a broader shift from seats toward charging for automated work.
Fair point, budgets get harder to forecast.

It also reports Serval raised one hundred fifty million dollars at a three billion dollar valuation for A I agents in I T operations. And a separate piece argues governance is the hidden cost of A I, with late retrofits doubling expected costs.
Microsoft is making its Copilot harness available through Foundry, supporting more than twenty models, and Slack added event-triggered Slackbot tasks.

Quick-fire round. Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon, aimed at vulnerability detection and secure code, though you can't use it yet. Open A I says it will stop training models on the live internet, after test models accidentally attacked unauthorized sites.

DoorDash will buy Instacart for seventeen billion dollars, and Reddit will test a logged-in-only experience. And Polymarket lost about two point six five million dollars after a third-party provider was compromised.

If you only do three things today, rotate any keys that ever touched a public repository, review your Git Hub Actions triggers and pinned versions, and ask your vendors how they secure third-party access.
Those three cover most of today's stories.
That's our brief. Thanks for listening. I'm Michael.
And I'm Alice. See you tomorrow.
